Text: {{c1::Mission-critical communications::category}} are any communications where a disruption will result in {{c2::failure of the task at hand}}, and their goal is an efficient, effective, error-free transfer of the {{c3::mental model}}.
Back Extra:
Why: when providers hold different pictures of "what's going on," situational awareness fails and errors begin.

Cue: think handoffs, radio reports, and team callouts.

Text: A {{c1::mental model::concept}} is the picture individuals have in their head of {{c2::"what's going on"}}, and a team works effectively only when all members {{c3::share the same one}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: a shared mental model means every team member, though in different roles seeing different things, holds the same picture of the situation.

Why: it is the very thing a good handoff transfers.

Text:
To build a shared mental model, a provider or team answers four questions in sequence:
1. {{c1::What is the focused priority for the patient?}} (the crux of the problem)
2. {{c1::What is the history of prior care?}} (what got us here)
3. {{c1::What is the patient's current state?}} (where are we now)
4. {{c1::What are the patient's immediate needs?}} (the very next thing that must happen)
Back Extra:
Why: answering these quickly gives the receiving clinicians a running start instead of restarting the assessment from scratch.

Cue: priority to history to current state to next need.

Text: {{c1::Patient care handover (handoff)::event}} is the transfer of both {{c2::pertinent patient information}} and the {{c3::responsibility for the patient's care}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: the American College of Emergency Physicians calls handover "the most dangerous point in a patient's ED journey."

Pitfall: it often involves physically moving the patient and equipment, adding to the risk.

Text:
The five-point method for giving a handover report:
{{c1::Initiate eye contact}}
{{c1::Manage the environment}}
{{c1::Ensure the ABCs}}
{{c1::Provide a structured report}}
{{c1::Provide documentation}}
Back Extra:
Cue: eye contact signals "we are communicating now, you and I."

Distinguish: "Ensure the ABCs" means any immediately needed or ongoing lifesaving care (e.g., CPR) is conveyed and continued first, before the full report.

Text: The structured handover mnemonic {{c1::SBAR}} stands for {{c2::Situation, Background, Assessment, and Recap/Rx}} (modified in EMS to SBAT, where the T is Treatment).
Back Extra:
Meaning: Situation = concise statement of the problem; Background = brief relevant info; Assessment = your findings and impression; Treatment/Recap = care already given.

Why: a standardized format greatly improves efficiency and reduces handoff errors.

Text:
The five-point method for receiving a handover report:
{{c1::Maintain eye contact}}
{{c1::Manage the environment}}
{{c1::Ensure understanding}}
{{c1::Summarize}}
{{c1::Gather supplementary patient documentation}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: "Summarize" means stating the receiver's mental model aloud so the reporting provider can catch and correct any errors.

Pitfall: the summary is not a repeat of the whole report, just the key mental-model recap.
